food.text: Sheikh Ahmad Qomi was a Persian-born merchant, born about 1543, who settled in the Ayutthaya Kingdom in the early 17th century. He set up a trading establishment, took a Thai wife and became quite wealthy. He is sometimes credited with introducing the popular Massaman curry to Thailand.

In the 17th century, European merchants exported wine from the Iranian city of Shiraz, and the trade has been documented. English and French travellers of the 17th to 19th centuries wrote enthusiastically about it. By the 9th century the city had already become Iran's wine capital.

Typical Iranian main dishes combine rice with meat, vegetables and nuts. Cooks also made abundant use of fruits alongside meats and in rice dishes, including plums, pomegranates, quince, prunes, apricots, barberries and raisins. Saffron, cardamom and dried lime gave characteristic flavours.

Kuku is an Iranian dish of whipped eggs with other ingredients folded in. It is cooked over low heat and served hot or cold with bread and either yogurt or salad. In Gilan, where rice was traditionally preferred to bread, it is often eaten with rice instead.

Travellers reported that the best Shiraz wines came from terraced vineyards around the village of Khollar, not from the vines nearest the city. The wine grown close to Shiraz was more dilute because of irrigation. The Khollar wines were white.

On the southern coast of the Caspian Sea, in provinces such as Gilan and Mazanderan, the fertile land shaped the local cooking. Kateh, a method of cooking rice, originates there. Caviar also comes from this region and was served with eggs in omelettes or simply eaten with lavash and butter.

Where the merchant Sheikh Ahmad came from in Persia is disputed. He is sometimes said to be from the city of Qom, but his descendant Tej Bunnag claimed he hailed from a town called Guni in the Mazandaran and Astarabad region south of the Caspian Sea.

Khollar's white wines came in two styles: dry wines for drinking young, and sweet wines meant for aging. Travellers compared the sweet ones to an old sherry, one of the most prized European wines of the day. At five years of age they were said to have a fine bouquet and nutty flavour.

In Gilan, Caspian kutum fish is a staple, usually served fried with rice. Smoked fish is also popular there and is often steamed together with the rice. Local people also eat medlar, which they call konos.

Herb kuku, called kuku sabzi, is the most popular kind of kuku and is traditionally served at Nowruz, the Iranian New Year. It is made of eggs and herbs such as leeks and parsley, and it symbolizes a fresh start.

art.text: Around 1510, a Venetian merchant named Domenico Romano visited the Hasht Behesht Palace in Tabriz, whose name means Palace of the Eight Paradises. He described an octagonal, two-story building topped by a dome, with a hall surrounded by thirty-two chambers and several terraces.

After the Battle of Tabriz in 1514, the Ottomans briefly occupied and looted the Hasht Behesht Palace. Many precious goods from the palace, along with artists from the Tabriz court, were sent to Istanbul.

Although the Ottomans destroyed the Hasht Behesht Palace, it remained hugely influential in the creation of other buildings in Iran. Among them was the Hasht Behesht in Isfahan, and the palace also helped shape the wider "Hasht Bihisht" model of architecture.

The Venetian visitor Domenico Romano marvelled that the palace's ground floor had four entrances and many apartments, all enameled and gilt in various ways. He wrote that it was so beautiful that he could hardly find words to express it.

The Hasht Behesht Palace was decorated with realistic scenes of past events, including an Ottoman embassy visiting Uzun Hasan and his hunting expeditions. Its color palette relied on gold, silver, and ultramarine blue.

The Hasht Behesht Palace appears in schematic form in some early Safavid paintings, such as Nighttime in a City, dated circa 1540 from Tabriz. The palace also appears on a 1538 map of Tabriz made by the Ottoman geographer Matrakçı Nasuh.
In 1585 the Ottoman Jafar Pasha destroyed the Hasht Behesht Palace. In its place he built the Castle of Jafar Pasha, a massive defensive structure.

Iranian music reached India through the 16th-century Persianate Mughal Empire. The Mughal court promoted new musical forms by bringing Iranian musicians there. Iranian music also built up much of the musical terminology of neighboring Turkic and Arabic cultures.

war.text: The zamburak was a small cannon mounted on a camel and fired by its rider, the zamburakchi. The name means 'little wasp' in Persian. This form of artillery was used in the Iranian army from the 17th century to the early 20th century.

In 1622 the Safavids conquered Hormuz with the help of the English. The Portuguese had occupied the island from 1515 to 1622. Afterward the Safavids tried to expel the Portuguese from the rest of the Persian Gulf.

On 13 February 1739, Nader Shah won a decisive victory at the Battle of Karnal during his invasion of India, attracted by India's wealth and knowing the Mughals were much weaker. His forces defeated the numerically superior army of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in about three hours. The victory paved the way for the Persian sack of Delhi, where Nader issued orders for a general massacre and his army completely sacked and looted the city. Muhammad Shah had to beg Nader to grant him and his people mercy, handing over the keys of the city and the royal treasury, which included the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor.

In 1795 Agha Mohammad Khan moved on Tbilisi to restore Persian dominion over Georgia, after seeing the Treaty of Georgievsk as defiance. At the Battle of Krtsanisi, Heraclius II could muster only around 5,000 troops, and the Georgians lost 4,000 men, while the Iranians lost 13,000, a third of their force. Tbilisi was completely sacked and its population massacred, including the archbishop Doistheus, and about 15,000 captives were carried off. An eyewitness who entered days later described a road paved with corpses, women and children slaughtered by the sword, over a thousand men dead in a single tower, and a burned city whose putrefying bodies gave off an intolerable, infectious stench.

The Russo-Persian Wars began in 1651 and continued intermittently until 1828. They consisted of five conflicts, all rooted in disputed governance of the Caucasus. The Treaty of Turkmenchay ended the War of 1826 to 1828, when the Persians ceded much of their Transcaucasian holdings to Russia.

In 1629, Grand Vizier Gazi Hüsrev Pasha mustered Ottoman forces, but a severe winter and heavy floods made operations in central Iraq impossible. He turned east and invaded Persia proper. On 4 May 1630 he routed the Persians under Zainal Khan Begdeli Shamlu at Mahidasht near Kermanshah, then sacked the city of Hamadan.

Agha Mohammed Khan raised an army of 60,000 men for his 1795 campaign and divided it into three, simultaneously attacking Shirvan, Erivan, and the fortress at Shusha. He took Tiflis, and in the invasion thousands of Georgians were massacred and 15,000 citizens were taken into captivity and sent as slaves to Persia. Erekle II fled from Tiflis.

Shah Abbas wanted to retake Kandahar, which he had lost in 1595. In 1621 he ordered an army to gather at Nishapur, and he reached Kandahar on 20 May and began the siege. The small Mughal garrison of 3,000 men could not hold for long against the superior Persian army.
During the late Safavid period there were 3,000 zamburaks. Nader Shah used them in his invasion of India between 1738 and 1739. In a military parade in 1739/40, 1,700 zamburaks were present.

Russia did not intervene to protect Heraclius II, even though the Treaty of Georgievsk of 1783 promised it would. Catherine the Great later launched a punitive campaign against Iran in 1796, but it was recalled after her death the same year. The shah was assassinated in Shusha in 1797.

In 1602 the Persian army under Allahverdi Khan, by order of Abbas I, expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain. Portuguese rule there had ended after the Hormuzi governor, a relative of the Hormuzi king, started executing members of Bahrain's leading families. In 1624 the Portuguese helped the Ottoman pasha of Basra repel a Persian invasion: a fleet of galleys packed with cannons and infantry bombarded the Safavid army's camps until the casualties were so high that the Safavids retreated.

The zamburakchis' musical branch played a different role than in Western armies, where soldiers marched in rhythm to drumbeats, sometimes with martial tunes that kept them in pace. The purpose of the zamburakchis' musicians was to irritate the enemy soldiers. A Persian expression, 'like the zanburkhaneh camel', described someone used to loud noises, suggesting that the camel had endured so many blasts on its back that it no longer reacted.

literature.text: Azerbaijani literature developed greatly after Iran's first reunification in 800 years under the Safavid Empire. The Safavid rulers themselves wrote poetry. It shows how court culture shaped literary life in this era.

Under the Safavids, literature and Persian poetry linked the pre-Islamic past to the present. They served as shared cultural traditions for both common people and the elite, especially in cities. The legendary kings of the Shahnameh, battling eternal forces of evil, were tied to the Islamic Safavid present.

A magnificent copy of the Shahnameh, the epic "Book of Kings", was made during Shah Tahmasp's reign. It is described as a stellar example of manuscript illumination and calligraphy. It shows how the national epic was celebrated as a work of art as well as literature.

Some modern Iranian scholars suggest calling Sabk-i Hindi by the names sabk-i Isfahani or sabk-i Safavi instead. Their reason is that poets of the Safavid court in Isfahan during the 17th and early 18th century wrote in a similar manner.

Another famous manuscript was the Khamsa by Nizami, executed between 1539 and 1543 by Agha Mirak and his school in Isfahan. Like the Shahnameh made under Shah Tahmasp, it shows how classic Persian poetry was preserved in lavishly crafted books.

Iase Tushi settled in Isfahan in the early 17th century and wrote Samecniero ("Scientific"), the earliest Georgian manuscript discovered in Iran. The poem describes biblical stories from an Islamic perspective. It also contains one of the first Georgian-Persian dictionaries.

The Zoroastrian text Saddar Nazm, written in 1495 by Mardshah ibn Malekshah, expanded on the older Saddar Nasr. In 1700 it was translated by Thomas Hyde. That made it among the earliest Zoroastrian texts known to Western scholars.

Parsadan Gorgijanidze, a politician and historian in the Safavid Empire, wrote a Georgian version of the Iranian epic Shahnameh called Rostomiani ("Stories of Rostom"). He also produced an account of the history of Georgia in Isfahan in the 1690s.

The Frenchman Anquetil Duperron first translated the Vendidad in 1759, working with Zoroastrian texts brought from Bombay, India. Western study of Avestic and ancient Persian literature began in the 18th century. Sir William Jones and Sylvestre de Sacy later worked on Pahlavi texts.

science.text: The zamburak was foreign military technology adapted to local conditions. Because it was mounted directly on a camel rather than on a carriage, it allowed greater mobility and versatility. Zamburaks could be fired from a moving camel, but were often fired from a sitting one.
The Safavid dynasty ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736, and its rule is often considered the beginning of modern Iranian history. It is also counted as one of the gunpowder empires.
During the late Safavid period, Iran fielded 3,000 zamburaks. A unit called the zamburak-khana was eventually formed to manage them, and it was commanded by an officer known as the zamburakchi-bashi.
The zamburak may have been in use in Safavid Iran as early as the 16th century. It first appears in Iranian writings during the reign of Shah Abbas I, who ruled from 1587 to 1629.

During the early Qajar period, Iran remained behind other powers in weapon technology. Apart from the zamburak, its artillery consisted mainly of weapons captured from the Portuguese in 1622 and from the Russians in 18th-century wars. By about 1800, under Fath-Ali Shah Qajar, around 1,500 zamburaks remained, and the weapon had become outdated.

politics.text: In 1501 the Safavid dynasty began ruling Iran, and Shah Ismail I established Twelver Shi'ism as the official religion of the empire. After conquering Iran and Azerbaijan, Ismail I made conversion mandatory for the largely Sunni population, and the Sunni Ulema, or clergy, were either killed or exiled. The source article calls this one of the most important turning points in the history of Islam. The dynasty lasted until 1736, though some place its end at 1722.

In 1709 Mirwais Hotak led a successful rebellion against the declining Safavid empire around Kandahar. His Ghilji Pashtun dynasty went on to rule parts of Iran and Afghanistan during the 1720s. Mirwais's son Mahmud, who overthrew the Safavid Shah and established his own rule over Iran, murdered his uncle Abdul Aziz, Mirwais's brother and successor, after Abdul Aziz had ruled only eighteen months. The dynasty was troubled and violent from the start, with bloody succession feuds.

Nader Shah deposed the last Safavid in 1736 and proclaimed himself Shah, founding the Afsharid dynasty. Under him Iran reached its greatest extent since the Sasanian Empire. After his death most of the empire was divided between the Zands, Durranis, and Khanate of Kalat.
When the Safavids captured the Iranian throne in 1501, the source of royal legitimacy changed from the Chinggisids to the Alids. Ismail I declared his support for Shia Islam that same year.

The Safavids became the first native dynasty since the Buyids to establish a national state officially known as Iran. They started from their base in Ardabil and reasserted the Iranian identity of the region.

The Safavid army was built mainly from the Qizilbash, meaning 'red-heads', who were Turkoman tribes. Their power was dangerous even to the court: Qizilbash leaders took part in intrigues, assassinating Shah Ismail II. When a Persian vakil was given command of a Safavid army in Transoxiana, the Qizilbash deserted him on the battlefield and he was slain; another vakil was murdered by them and a fifth put to death by them. Ethnic Iranians, including the Shahs, held the bureaucratic and cultural positions and led the empire politically as its administrative and religious elite.

Nader Shah invaded northern India with a fifty-five thousand strong army and defeated the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal in less than three hours. In March 1739 he attacked Delhi, which was sacked and looted after he ordered a general massacre. Muhammad Shah had to beg for mercy and hand over the city's keys and the royal treasury, which included the Peacock throne and the Koh-i-Noor.

After the death of Karim Khan Zand in 1779, Agha Mohammad Khan defeated all competitors from the Zand and Afsharid dynasties and unified Iran. Agha Mohammad Khan was known as one of the cruelest kings, even by the standards of 18th-century Iran. In his quest for power he razed cities, massacred entire populations, and blinded some 20,000 men in Kerman because its people had chosen to defend the city against his siege. He was formally crowned Shah in 1796 and was assassinated the next year, succeeded by his nephew Fath-Ali Shah.
After the Safavids, later dynasties took different religious paths. The Afsharid dynasty (1736 to 1796) mixed Shi'a and Sunni, while the Zand dynasty (1750 to 1794) was Twelver Shia.

When the Safavids took the Iranian throne in 1501, the source of legitimacy changed from the Chinggisids to the Alids. Leaders of the Safavid order had already claimed descent from Muhammad's family, and they altered the Safvat al-safa, a hagiography of Safi al-Din Ardabili, so that the family's Sunni Kurdish background became Arab descent from Muhammad.

In 1709 Mirwais and his men ambushed Gurgin Khan on 21 April, while he was away campaigning against the Kakar tribe, and killed him. The Georgians had ruled Kandahar with brutality towards the local population and were hated throughout the province. Mirwais's men expelled the Georgian garrison, and the surviving Georgians fled to Gereshk. The Safavid court sent Kaikhosro Khan with 12,000 men, but the army progressed slowly because the court was unwilling to help much. In 1711 Kaikhosro besieged Kandahar and refused the Ghilzais' offer of peace. When the Baluchis forced the Georgians to retreat, the defenders of Kandahar pursued them and killed Kaikhosro.

Nader Shah forced the Russians to give up territories they had taken in 1722–23, through the Treaty of Resht of 1732 and the Treaty of Ganja of 1735. He then continued the war against the Ottomans, and the 1736 Treaty of Constantinople forced them to confirm Iranian suzerainty over the Caucasus and recognise Nader as the new Shah.

In 1733 Nader's army was routed near Baghdad by the Ottoman general Topal Osman Pasha, and revolts were already breaking out in Iran, which Nader felt he had to answer quickly to save his position. He faced Topal again with a larger force and defeated and killed him. He later won a decisive victory over a superior Ottoman force at Yeghevard, and by the summer of 1735 Armenia and Georgia were under his rule.

philosophy.text: Mulla Sadra, born around 1571 or 1572, was an Iranian Twelver Shi'i mystic, philosopher and theologian who led the cultural renaissance in Iran during the 17th century. Oliver Leaman calls him arguably the single most important and influential philosopher in the Muslim world in the last four hundred years.

Mulla Sadra called his own philosophy the Transcendent Theosophy. It ambitiously combined Avicennism, Suhrawardi's Illuminationist philosophy, Ibn Arabi's Sufi metaphysics and Sunni Ash'ari theology within the framework of Twelver Shi'ism.

In 1591 Mulla Sadra moved to Qazvin, and in 1597 to Isfahan, to study philosophy, theology, Hadith and hermeneutics. Each city was at that time the Safavid capital and a center of Twelver Shi'ite seminaries. His teachers included Mir Damad and Baha' ad-Din al-'Amili.

Mulla Sadra is credited with a major transition from essentialism to existentialism in Islamic philosophy. His existentialism was a question of cosmology as it pertained to God, so it differs considerably from the individual, moral and social questions at the heart of Russian, French, German or American Existentialism.

In 1612 Ali Quli Khan, the powerful governor of Fars, asked Mulla Sadra to end his exile and return to Shiraz. There he taught and ran a newly built madrasa called the Khan School. Mulla Sadra spent the rest of his life teaching the intellectual sciences, especially his own Transcendent Theosophy.

Mulla Sadra's philosophical encyclopedia, the Transcendent Philosophy of the Four Journeys of the Intellect, drew on thinkers from Pythagoras to his own contemporaries. He began writing it around 1605, and it took almost 25 years to finish, until some years after 1630.

Si Asl is Mulla Sadra's only extant book of philosophy in Persian. In it he relies on three main moral principles to discuss moral and educative subjects related to scientists, and he offers advice to his contemporary philosophers.
Mulla Sadra also wrote Sharh-i Shafa, a commentary on some of the issues in the theology (Ilahiyyat) section of Ibn-Sina's al-Shifa.

culture.text: In 1501 the Safavid dynasty took control of Iran and made Shia Islam the state religion. Historians count this among the most important events in Islamic history. Until the 16th century, Iran had enjoyed a golden age of the arts and sciences.

Shah Ismail I established the Twelver denomination of Shi'a Islam as the official religion of the Persian Empire. The source calls this one of the most important turning points in the history of Islam. The Safavids also spread Shi'a Islam across parts of Central Asia, the Caucasus, Anatolia and the Persian Gulf.

The Safavid dynasty grew out of a Sufi order established in the city of Ardabil. From there the Safavids took control of parts of Greater Iran. They became the first native dynasty since the Sasanian Empire to establish a national state officially known as Iran.

Safavid rulers ruled over a population whose elite shared a broadly similar Turco-Persian culture with the Ottoman, Uzbek and Mughal empires. People across West, Central and South Asia shared common institutions, arts, knowledge, customs and rituals. Poets, artists, architects and scholars kept ties among far-flung cities such as Isfahan and Tabriz.

The Safavid dynasty grew out of a dervish order of Sufism, the Safavid order. Its leaders met violent ends: Junayd was killed during an incursion into the territories of the Shirvanshah, and Haydar was killed by Ya'qub in 1488, who also pursued and killed Haydar's son Ali Mirza Safavi. From its base in Ardabil, the order took control over parts of Greater Iran, and its shahs later made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, with the Safavids playing a crucial role in forcefully making it the official religion.

Jewish silk farmers were common in the Persian town of Lar. When the French traveler Jean-Baptiste Thévenot visited Larestan in 1687, he reported that most of Lar's inhabitants were Jewish silk farmers. Silk farming was also the work of Georgian Jewish deportees in Māzanderān, who were deported there and employed as silk worm farmers.

In 1606, during the Ottoman-Safavid War, Abbas I resettled some 300,000 Armenians deeper within Iran. He also gave them their own quarter in the then-capital Isfahan, the New Julfa district, which is still largely populated by Christian Armenians four centuries later.

The Safavids altered a hagiography of Safi al-Din Ardabili, the Safvat al-safa, which Ibn Bazzaz had composed in 1350. In the changes, the Sunni Kurdish background of the family became an Arab descent from Muhammad. Their full lineage was still not made clear.
